newsitem.title: UK: British unions face threat of new strike curbs.
newsitem.headline: British unions face threat of new strike curbs.

text.p: Britain unveiled proposals on Tuesday for sweeping new curbs on strikes that even former prime minister Margaret Thatcher shied away from in the 1980s when she set out to cut trade unions down to size.

The cornerstone of the plan, which is in response to a summer of disruptions to the postal service and London Underground services, allows unions to be sued if a strike causes "disproportionate or excessive effects."
For example, a commuter left with no way of getting to work due to a train strike or a firm that lost an important contract because of mail delays would be able to sue for damages.
"The right to strike has to be reconciled with the need to protect the public from being severely disrupted," said Trade Secretary Ian Lang, introducing a consultative "green" paper.

He proposed doubling the notice period for a strike to 14 days, requiring a strike to be approved by a majority of those entitled to vote -- instead of a majority of those voting -- and requiring new strike ballots every three months during a long-running industrial action.
The number of days lost to strikes in Britain had fallen by 90 percent since Thatcher started to reform Britain's industrial relations laws in 1979, Lang said.
But a problem remained in monopoly public-sector industries. The post and railway strikes meant more working days were lost in August alone than in the whole of 1994 or 1995, he said.
"In deciding on industrial action, trade unions and their members pursuing a particular dispute must take account of the broader interests of the community," Lang said.
Initial reaction to the plan was hostile.
David Blunkett, the opposition Labour party's education and employment spokesman, said many of the proposals figured in Thatcher's 1983 manifesto and in a 1981 consultation paper.
But they were never implemented for sound practical reasons such as the difficulty of defining a "disproportionate" effect.

"Today's Green Paper has nothing to do with preventing or resolving disputes, and everything to do with playing politics on the issue. Individuals and business will not gain from these proposals -- the only gainers will be the lawyers," he said.
The Institute of Management said Lang's proposals would do nothing to curb strikes and accused him of overreacting.

"The proposals do not make clear what are "disproportionate or excessive' effects. This legislation could mean employers and employees spending more time in the court than around the negotiating table," IOM director general Roger Young said.
Lew Adams, general secretary of train drivers' union ASLEF, said the proposals were "just an election ploy designed to raise the temperature."
